Jobs and the Job Manager

Every background task SATOM runs — and every action that talks to an appliance — is a job you can watch, pause, stop and inspect, from the Jobs page, the toast dock or a dedicated wait page.

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user
📍 WhereSidebar → Operations → Jobs (Global console: Global → Jobs) (URL /jobs/manager)

What is it?#

A job is a unit of background work with a status, a progress bar, an owner and a log. Firmware image verification, bulk applies, monitoring sweeps — and, above all, every POST that acts on an appliance — run as jobs, so a slow device never freezes a button or times out a page half-way through a change.

You follow jobs in three places: the Jobs page (the Job Manager), the toast dock in the bottom-right corner of every page, and — for a classic form whose device action takes a while — a dedicated wait page.

What does it do?#

  • Lists every running and finished job with its status, progress, owner, where it runs (server host and process id, appliance) and duration.
  • Lets you Pause, Resume and Stop a job. Control is cooperative: SATOM sets a flag and the worker obeys it at its next safe checkpoint, so a write already in flight to a device is never cut in half.
  • Shows, for device actions, one step per call to the device (GET /api/v2.0/cmdb/server-policy/policy · 200 · 0.4 s), so you can see where a slow action is.
  • Queues writes to the same appliance behind each other, so two people pushing to one box at once cannot interleave their changes.
  • Replays the action's own response (redirect, page, JSON or file download, including its flash messages) once a long device action finishes.
  • Marks jobs left "running" by a service restart as failed instead of letting them haunt the dock forever.
  1. 1You press a buttonThe POST is wrapped and replayed inside a job thread
  2. 2Inline window (2 s)A fast action answers normally — no job is visible
  3. 3Still running?You get a toast (scripted pages) or the wait page (classic forms)
  4. 4Steps & queueEach device call becomes a step; a second write to the same box waits
  5. 5FinishedThe original response is replayed; the dock shows success, error or stopped

Requirements#

  • You must be signed in. No other permission is needed to see your own jobs.
  • Device actions run as jobs only on the primary node. On a standby, and for API-token (Bearer) callers, the action runs inline as before (see What is excluded).

Permissions#

The Jobs page and its endpoints require only a signed-in session.

Who Sees Can control
Any signed-in user Their own jobs (jobs whose owner is their user name) Pause / Resume / Stop their own jobs
A user with users.manage (Administrator) Every user's jobs — the page header says "You are seeing all users' jobs." Pause / Resume / Stop anyone's job

Jobs are additionally filtered by ADOM: a job stamped with a product is listed only in a console that can see that product.

A job owned by someone else answers 404 not found rather than 403. The response of a device action (/jobs/<id>/response) is restricted to the job's owner even for administrators, because it can contain device configuration.

How to use#

Open the Job Manager#

  1. In the sidebar open Operations → Jobs (in the Global console: Global → Jobs). The page is also linked from the Global home page and from All jobs → on an appliance's Jobs on this device card.
  2. The table refreshes itself every 3 seconds; the badge next to the title shows how many jobs match.
  3. Narrow the list with the All states dropdown, the Filter by title, type, user, device… box, or the Active only switch.
  4. Click a row (or the expand button) to see its detail: the list of Steps (for device actions, the last 200 calls) and the full job record as JSON, with a Copy button. Click the job ID to copy it.

A link of the form /jobs/manager?focus=<job id> (used by View job → in the dock) opens the page with that job expanded and highlighted.

Pause, resume or stop a job#

  1. In the Actions column press Pause, Resume or Stop.
  2. Stop asks "Stop this job? It will halt at its next safe checkpoint." The status turns to Stopping…, then Stopped.
  3. A job that can no longer be interrupted shows a locked chip instead of the buttons.
Status label Meaning
Pending Created, worker not started yet
Running Working
Pausing… Pause requested; the worker has not reached a checkpoint yet
Paused Parked at a safe checkpoint — "Paused — waiting at a safe checkpoint"
Stopping… Stop requested; finishing the current step
Stopped Ended by a Stop. Not a failure
Success Finished normally
Error Failed, or orphaned by a restart

Follow a device action#

When an action on an appliance takes longer than the inline window (2 seconds by default):

  • On a scripted page (buttons that call the server in the background) a toast appears in the dock and follows you across pages. When the job ends, the page that started it receives the real answer as if it had come back immediately.
  • On a classic form you land on the wait page (/jobs/<id>/wait): a progress bar, the current message, every device call as it happens, and the buttons Stop (while it is still safe), Keep working — it continues in the background, Open in Jobs and Show result. When the action finishes, the page hands over to the action's own response — the redirect, page or file you would have got inline. Leaving the page stops nothing.

The appliance detail page also has a Jobs on this device card listing the running and most recent jobs for that box ("Every action on this device runs as a job; the running and most recent ones appear here.").

Use the toast dock#

Each foreground job you own gets a toast in the bottom-right corner:

  • Stop — shown only while the server says the job is cancelable.
  • − (Minimize) — shrinks the toast to one line with the title, the percentage and a thin bar. Press □ (Restore) or click the title to bring it back. The minimised state survives page changes and a full reload of the tab.
  • × (Dismiss) — removes the toast; the job keeps running and stays on the Jobs page.
  • When the job ends the toast turns green, red or amber and offers View job →, plus Show result → for an action that produced a page or a file, or View before/after report → when the job produced a report. It dismisses itself after 12 s (success), 15 s (stopped) or 20 s (error) — 60 s when a report or a mid-change warning is attached.

Monitoring sweeps and other housekeeping marked background never get a toast; they appear only on the Jobs page, and a failure still reaches the notification bell.

Configuration#

Setting Description Required Example
SATOM_JOB_INLINE_S Seconds a device action may run inline before it becomes a visible job. Default 2.0 No 2.0
SATOM_DEVICE_LOCK_MAX_WAIT_S How long a queued write waits for another job's lock on the same device before giving up. Default 1800 No 1800
SATOM_DEVICE_JOBS 0 / false / off / no disables device jobs entirely; every action runs inline No 1

These are environment variables of the web service (see Configuration files).

Example#

🧪Example — Two operators push to the same FortiWeb

Alice saves a server policy on fweb-01; the save makes several REST calls. Thirty seconds later Bob applies a protection profile to the same box. Bob's job shows Queued — waiting for "Save object (objedit) · fweb-01" on this device and its toast title ends in — queued. Bob can still Stop it — nothing has been sent. When Alice's job finishes, Bob's job takes the device lock, its Stop button disappears (a multi-call write cannot be stopped half-way), and its steps start appearing.

Result#

  • A job record is written under data/jobs/<id>.json. A device action that answered inside the inline window and never reached a device leaves no record — a validation error or a pure database edit does not clutter the list.
  • A device action's final response is stored under data/jobs/responses/ so it can be replayed (maximum 50 MB; larger bodies are not kept).
  • The job's progress reflects real calls: an action with known phases shows a phased bar; otherwise the bar creeps towards 95 % per call and never claims completion early.

Troubleshooting#

"This task cannot be stopped once started."#

Possible causes - The job is flagged non-cancelable (for example a firmware flash that is already rebooting the box). - A device write job has taken the device lock: from that moment stopping it between two calls would leave the appliance half-changed.

Solution 1. Wait for the job to finish; follow it on the Jobs page. 2. If it fails, review the steps in its detail to see which calls succeeded.

Verification — the job reaches Success, Error or Stopped.

"Only a running job can be paused." / "This job is not paused."#

Possible causes — the job already finished, or is already stopping.

Solution — refresh the Jobs page; use Resume only on a Paused or Pausing… job.

A job says "Queued — waiting for … on this device"#

Possible causes — another write job holds the lock on the same appliance.

Solution 1. Open Open in Jobs and look for the job named in the message. 2. Let it finish, or stop it if it is still stoppable. The queued job starts automatically. Stop is always safe while a job is queued.

Verification — the queued label disappears and steps begin to appear.

"Gave up after 1800 s waiting for another action on this device to finish."#

Possible causes — the device lock was held for longer than SATOM_DEVICE_LOCK_MAX_WAIT_S.

Solution — find the long-running job on the same appliance, wait for it or stop it, then repeat your action.

"Orphaned — the service restarted while this job was running."#

Possible causes — the web service restarted (update, crash, reboot) while the job's worker thread was alive. Workers are threads inside the web process; a restart kills them without updating the job file.

Solution — check on the device whether the change was applied (for device actions: the steps list shows which calls completed) and repeat the action if needed.

A toast keeps reappearing for a job that is clearly dead#

Possible causes — a "ghost" job whose worker never started.

Solution 1. The feed sweeps ghosts automatically at most every 2 minutes; wait and navigate once. 2. On the server: sudo satom get job list shows the ledger including ghosts; sudo satom execute repair jobs --yes sweeps them (see below).

"the response was too large to keep" / "this job has no stored response"#

Possible causes — the action's response exceeded 50 MB, or the job was not a device action, or its response was pruned.

Solution — repeat the action; for a large export use the feature's own download.

Advanced#

What is excluded#

Advanced Device actions that do not become jobs

Device-job wrapping applies to POST routes of these areas: appliance lifecycle (appliances, console, upgrade flow, device and system provisioning, backups, backup import), FortiWeb configuration (workspace, object editor, policy wizard, web protection, server objects, exceptions, section configuration, structure, segments, signatures, line profiles, certificate manager, templates, change requests), FortiADC / FortiAnalyzer / FortiAuthenticator pages and their API pages, and the investigation tools that query a box (attack search, transaction tracer, Lua Studio, API explorer, analysis, logs, Path Diagnostics, reachability batch, config compare, artifacts, container operations, Sentinel, deep monitor, service monitor).

Excluded endpoints (they stay synchronous):

Endpoint Why
appliances.upgrade_push, appliances.downgrade_push already a background job (the flash job)
appliances.rediscover_start own worker, mirrored into a job by the rediscovery service
appliances.rediscover_stop control for a running sweep; must answer at once
backups.create_backup already a background job
deep_monitor.run, deep_monitor.discover already a background job
service_monitor.run, service_monitor.discover already a background job
signatures.sync already a background job
console.bundle streams a support bundle download

Pass-through (no job is created even for a wrapped route): non-POST requests, API-token (Bearer) callers, a standby node, the test suite, and SATOM_DEVICE_JOBS=0.

Areas outside that list — for example Scheduled Actions Run now, Process runs, Settings — run inside the request as before.

Advanced Read versus write, and the per-device lock

An action is classified from its endpoint name. Names containing only read words (preview, check, test, compare, list, export, fetch, status…) are reads: they never queue and stay stoppable between calls. Any write word (save, apply, push, delete, restore, upgrade, approve, run…) makes it a write — the safe side wins, so failover_preflight is a write.

A write job takes the device lock on its first call to that device (an flock on a file under data/jobs/locks/, keyed by the appliance's address). The lock works across all web workers and is released by the kernel if a worker dies, so a crash never leaves a device locked. A job holds at most one device lock and only waits while it holds none, so two jobs cannot deadlock.

Advanced Storage, sweeping and retention
  • Job state is one JSON file per job under data/jobs/, written atomically, so a poll landing on any web worker reads a consistent view.
  • Orphan sweep: at every service start and, throttled to once every 120 seconds, whenever the dock feed or the Job Manager is read. An active job is orphaned when its recorded process id is gone, or when it never recorded one and has not been updated for 10 minutes. Jobs recorded on another host are never touched.
  • Nothing prunes the job ledger automatically. Use sudo satom execute repair jobs [--older-than N] [--yes] (default 7 days): without --yes it shows what it would do; with it, it sweeps ghosts and deletes finished job records (and their stored responses) older than N days. See CLI.
  • Rollback: there is no universal undo. A job type that can compensate its own writes registers compensations as it goes and replays them newest-first on stop or failure; a stopped bulk job may report devices left mid-change, which the toast summarises as "N device(s) left mid-change, M write(s) to review".
